{{Short description|Concept in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''Noetherian scheme''' is a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] that admits a finite [[Cover (topology)|covering]] by [[open set|open]] affine subsets [[spectrum of a ring|<math>\operatorname{Spec} A_i</math>]], where each <math>A_i</math> is a [[Noetherian ring]]. More generally, a scheme is '''locally Noetherian''' if it is covered by spectra of Noetherian rings. Thus, a scheme is Noetherian if and only if it is locally Noetherian and [[compact space|compact]].  As with Noetherian rings, the concept is named after [[Emmy Noether]].

It can be shown that, in a locally Noetherian scheme, if&nbsp; <math>\operatorname{Spec} A</math> is an open affine subset, then ''A'' is a Noetherian ring; in particular, <math>\operatorname{Spec} A</math> is a Noetherian scheme if and only if ''A'' is a Noetherian ring. For a locally Noetherian scheme ''X,'' the [[local ring]]s <math>\mathcal{O}_{X, x}</math> are also Noetherian rings.

A Noetherian scheme is a [[Noetherian topological space]]. But the converse is false in general; consider, for example, the spectrum of a non-Noetherian [[valuation ring]].

The definitions extend to [[formal scheme]]s.

== Properties and Noetherian hypotheses ==
Having a (locally) Noetherian hypothesis for a statement about schemes generally makes a lot of problems more accessible because they sufficiently rigidify many of its properties.

Any Noetherian scheme can only have finitely many [[irreducible component]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lemma 28.5.7 (0BA8)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BA8|access-date=2020-07-24|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref>

Every [[morphism of schemes|morphism]] from a Noetherian scheme <math>X \to S</math> is [[Quasi-compact morphism|quasi-compact]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lemma 28.5.8 (01P0)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01P0|access-date=2020-07-24|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref>

=== Dévissage ===
One of the most important structure theorems about Noetherian rings and Noetherian schemes is the [[Dévissage|dévissage theorem]]. This makes it possible to decompose arguments about [[Coherent sheaf|coherent sheaves]] into inductive arguments. Given a [[short exact sequence]] of coherent sheaves<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{E}'' \to 0,</math></blockquote>proving one of the sheaves has some property is equivalent to proving the other two have the property. In particular, given a fixed coherent sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and a sub-coherent sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}'</math>, showing <math>\mathcal{F}</math> has some property can be reduced to looking at <math>\mathcal{F}'</math> and <math>\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{F}'</math>. Since this process can only be non-trivially applied only a finite number of times, this makes many induction arguments possible.

=== Homological properties ===
There are many nice [[homology (mathematics)|homological]] properties of Noetherian schemes.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Cohomology of Sheaves|url=http://therisingsea.org/notes/Section3.2-CohomologyOfSheaves.pdf|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

==== Čech and sheaf cohomology ====
[[Čech cohomology]] and [[sheaf cohomology]] agree on an affine open cover. This makes it possible to compute the sheaf cohomology of <math>\mathbb{P}^n_S</math> using Čech cohomology for the standard open cover.

==== Compatibility of colimits with cohomology ====
Given a [[direct system]] <math>\{ \mathcal{F}_\alpha, \phi_{\alpha\beta} \}_{\alpha \in \Lambda}</math> of sheaves of abelian groups on a Noetherian scheme, there is a canonical isomorphism<blockquote><math>\varinjlim H^i(X,\mathcal{F}_\alpha) \to H^i(X, \varinjlim \mathcal{F}_\alpha)</math></blockquote>meaning the [[functor]]s<blockquote><math>H^i(X,-): \text{Ab}(X) \to \text{Ab}</math></blockquote>preserve direct limits and [[coproduct]]s.

==== Derived direct image ====
Given a [[locally of finite type|locally finite type]] morphism <math>f:X \to S</math> to a Noetherian scheme <math>S</math> and a complex of sheaves <math>\mathcal{E}^\bullet \in D^b_{Coh}(X)</math> with bounded [[coherent cohomology]] such that the sheaves <math>H^i(\mathcal{E}^\bullet)</math> have proper support over <math>S</math>, then the derived pushforward <math>\mathbf{R}f_*(\mathcal{E}^\bullet)</math> has bounded coherent cohomology over <math>S</math>, meaning it is an object in <math>D^b_{Coh}(S)</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lemma 36.10.3 (08E2)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08E2|access-date=2020-07-24|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref>

== Examples ==
Most schemes of interest are Noetherian schemes.

=== Locally of finite type over a Noetherian base ===
Another class of examples of Noetherian schemes<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lemma 29.15.6 (01T6)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01T6|access-date=2020-07-24|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu}}</ref> are families of schemes <math>X \to S</math> where the base <math>S</math> is Noetherian and <math>X</math> is of [[morphism of finite type|finite type]] over <math>S</math>. This includes many examples, such as the [[Connected component (topology)|connected component]]s of a [[Hilbert scheme]], i.e. with a fixed Hilbert polynomial. This is important because it implies many [[moduli space]]s encountered in the wild are Noetherian, such as the [[Moduli of algebraic curves]] and [[Moduli of stable vector bundles]]. Also, this property can be used to show many schemes considered in algebraic geometry are in fact Noetherian.

=== Quasi-projective varieties ===
In particular, quasi-projective varieties are Noetherian schemes. This class includes [[algebraic curve]]s, [[elliptic curve]]s, [[abelian varieties]], [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi-Yau schemes]], [[Shimura varieties]], [[K3 surface]]s, and [[cubic surface]]s. Basically all of the objects from classical algebraic geometry fit into this class of examples.

=== Infinitesimal deformations of Noetherian schemes ===
In particular, infinitesimal deformations of Noetherian schemes are again Noetherian. For example, given a curve <math>C / \text{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_q)</math>, any [[Deformation theory|deformation]] <math>\mathcal{C}/\text{Spec}(\mathbb{F}_{q}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^n))</math> is also a Noetherian scheme. A tower of such deformations can be used to construct formal Noetherian schemes.

=== Non-examples ===

==== Schemes over Adelic bases ====
One of the natural rings which are non-Noetherian are the [[ring of adeles]] <math>\mathbb{A}_K</math> for an [[algebraic number field]] <math>K</math>. In order to deal with such rings, a topology is considered, giving [[topological ring]]s. There is a notion of algebraic geometry over such rings developed by [[André Weil]] and [[Alexander Grothendieck]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Conrad|first=Brian|date=|title=Weil and Grothendieck Approaches to Adelic Points|url=http://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/adelictop.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721133058/http://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/adelictop.pdf|archive-date=21 July 2018|access-date=|website=}}</ref>

==== Rings of integers over infinite extensions ====
Given an infinite [[Galois field extension]] <math>K/L</math>, such as <math>\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_\infty)/\mathbb{Q}</math> (by adjoining all roots of unity), the [[ring of integers]] <math>\mathcal{O}_K</math> is a non-Noetherian ring which is dimension <math>1</math>. This breaks the intuition that finite dimensional schemes are necessarily Noetherian. Also, this example provides motivation for why studying schemes over a non-Noetherian base; that is, schemes <math>\text{Sch}/\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_E)</math>, can be an interesting and fruitful subject.

One special case<ref>{{Cite book|last=Neukirch|first=Jürgen|title=Algebraic Number Theory|date=1999|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-662-03983-0|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|chapter=1.13|oclc=851391469}}</ref><sup>pg 93</sup> of such an extension is taking the maximal unramified extension <math>K^{ur}/K</math> and considering the ring of integers <math>\mathcal{O}_{K^{ur}}</math>. The induced morphism<blockquote><math>\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{K^{ur}}) \to \text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)</math></blockquote>forms the [[universal covering]] of <math>\text{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_K)</math>.

==== Polynomial ring with infinitely many generators ====
Another example of a non-Noetherian finite-dimensional scheme (in fact zero-dimensional) is given by the following quotient of a polynomial ring with infinitely many generators.
<blockquote><math>\frac{\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots]}{(x_1,x_2^2,x_3^3,\ldots)}</math></blockquote>
